did_you_know.text: Did you know? The song opens with images from nature: “the rose of Sharon” and “the lily of the valleys.” The speaker describes herself through plants associated with beauty and delicacy.

Did you know? The beloved is compared to “an apple tree among the trees of the forest”—a prominent tree that provides shade among the forest trees. The speaker emphasizes the pleasure of sitting in its shade and the sweetness of its fruit.

Did you know? Three times in the Song of Songs, the “daughters of Jerusalem” are adjured not to awaken love before its time. In this chapter, the emphasis is on allowing love to develop until the appropriate time.
Did you know? The beloved’s movement is described with swift verbs: “leaping” and “bounding.” This creates a sense of energetic approach, like a gazelle moving lightly across the mountains and hills.

Did you know? The beloved’s invitation, “Arise, go... and come away,” is repeated later in the chapter, in verse 13. The repetition links the call to leave the sheltered place with nature’s awakening in spring.

Did you know? Verses 11–13 describe signs of spring: winter has passed, the rain is over, the blossoms have appeared, the voice of the turtledove is heard, the fig trees are beginning to ripen, and the vines give off their fragrance.
Did you know? The beloved asks the dove hiding in the clefts of the rock to show its appearance and let its voice be heard. The verse places two means of revelation side by side: sight and hearing.

Did you know? “The little foxes” are described as damaging the vineyards precisely when the vineyards are in bloom, “and our vineyards are in blossom.” The image conveys concern about harm coming to something young that is still growing.

Did you know? The statement “My beloved is mine, and I am his” presents clear mutuality between the beloved woman and her beloved. Their relationship is also portrayed through the image of shepherding “among the lilies.”

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the images of the gazelle and the young deer appear again, having already been used to describe the beloved’s movement in verses 8–9. This creates a circle of closeness, distance, and movement among the mountains.
